content.title: Server and Client Components
content.hook: React can run in different environments.
content.context:
In the App Router, components are Server Components by default. Client Components are used when the UI needs client-side capabilities such as state, event handlers, or browser-only APIs.

This gives us a boundary.
goals: Master Server and Client Components: Keep the boundary as small as the requirement allows.

activities.title: When does client code become necessary?

content.title: When does client code become necessary?
content.text:
Imagine:

```tsx
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
```

Now the component needs React state in the browser.

That is a signal that the component belongs on the client side.

content.title: The boundary is architectural
content.text:
Think of the tree:

```text
Page
├── Server-rendered content
└── Interactive button
```

The whole page does not need to become client-side just because one small piece is interactive.

A useful strategy is:

**Keep the boundary as small as the requirement allows.**

content.title: Client Components
content.text:
A Client Component begins with:

```tsx
'use client';
```

That tells the framework that the module belongs to the client side of the application.

content.question: Which component most clearly needs to be a Client Component?

options.text: A component using `useState` for an interactive menu

feedback.correct: Correct answer: B. A component using `useState` for an interactive menu
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: B. A component using `useState` for an interactive menu

content.title: What crosses the boundary?
content.text:
Do not treat the boundary like a magical wall.

It is a design decision about where code runs.

Client code can interact with users.

Server code can perform server-side work without shipping that work as browser JavaScript.
